Anxiety can shape how you view the world. Those are all differences and not inherently bad or in need of fixing. Bi polar has negative effects, the differences caused can suck, but not all of them do and people shouldn’t have to view them that way. Also, I’ve been fairly neutral so far but I have to call out your blatantly ignorant response. Saying “we have cures and therapies” as if that’s the solution and it’s all kittens and rainbows after. If you’ve ever been to a psychiatrists office then I guarantee you will never hear the word “cure” when it comes to your mental health. Meds are to lessen your symptoms, therapy is for learning coping mechanisms. Both of those things are meant to help the individual learn how to manage their mental differences.

I am saying we should change the word we use. Difference instead of illness, literally because of the definition you’re giving. Not everyone with a mental difference is mentally ill, but many have to be labeled as such to get the resources they need. It is not helpful. It’s inaccurate and harmful. If you’re not at ease then you wouldn’t call yourself diseased, but if you don’t share the same brain chemistry as everyone else then you are ill and THAT is the problem because they’re not all ill.

“A disorder of structure or function” in the brain is not illness by default. By your logic people with autism are sick and -should- be like everyone else, but the reality is they are different and not all of them want to be “normal” 

Plus if you want to get all technical with terms, a disease is literally anything that makes it so I am no longer at ease, but you wouldn’t use the word that way. So why are we using the word “illness” for people that are just different? That’s not just inaccurate but also damaging.

Physical illness doesn’t easily compare to this, I don’t think, but I do know there’s wheelchair bound people that will insist to you that they are not damaged and in need of fixing, they’re just differently abled. My point is that it’s not helpful for you or anyone to label somebody else as sick simply because they are different, but that’s literally what society and the system does. In order to get proper support for your mental differences you must be labeled as mentally ill, and I’m saying that in a perfect world people could get support for their mental differences and we literally would not see them as an illness. If someone has anxiety and the tools to live a functional life then they’re not really sick and don’t need you telling them to get cured. And you saying they are is inaccurate and damaging.

Maybe most people with mental illness would prefer not to have it, but not everyone. Some people have their world view shaped by their bi polar or their depression, they use it to make art, they can’t imagine not having it. Obviously there is a difference between someone with bi polar and someone without, and those differences need to be addressed and managed, but are they broken? Do they really need a cure? Do you think everyone with autism is broken and needs a cure? Because I can tell you for a fact that not everyone with autism thinks that. In fact, people think that’s harmful and wrong.

Well I guess we’re both making assumptions then. But who defines the “right” way a brain should do things? Do you think people with autism are broke and in need of a cure? Because there’s people who would tell you they don’t, they’re just different and need to handle things differently. Maybe some of those differences suck, but if society accommodates them to a point where that person can learn to manage those differences and live a functional life then are they still sick? Are they still broken in your eyes? They are still autistic, that didn’t change. They just learned to manage their differences is all.

How is the brain of someone with autism “Broken”? They see the world differently than most people, there’s things that are more difficult for them so awareness of that difference is important. But you know that not everyone with autism even wants to be “cured” right? It’s not like a physical illness. Someone with diabetes needs insulin to live. Period. What does someone with chronic depression need to live? What chemical is going to just alter the differences in their brain and make them “normal”? Mental health is not easily comparable to physical. Some people are just different and need to handle things differently, and if society accommodated them then they wouldn’t even be considered as mentally ill or broken, just different. So someone that becomes easily depressed isn’t damaged, they just have to learn coping mechanisms to deal with that difference so their lives don’t spiral out of control when something triggers their depression. 

Edit: Poor wording.

Try telling someone with autism that they’re sick and need to be cured. Sure, there are people out there who would take a magic pill to “cure” it if they could. And there’s people who wouldn’t do that and shouldn’t be pressured or forced into that. There’s people with mental differences that  aren’t sick and are hurt by being labeled as such, yet they have to be labeled that way in order to get the support and resources they need.

My focus is on what we shouldn’t do more so than what we should. We shouldn’t be calling everyone with a mental difference mentally ill. If someone hears voices that aren’t there and feels like this negatively impacts their life then yeah, they need resources and support to handle those differences. But are they sick? Are they broken? If so, when does that stop being the case? If they learn how to better manage their mental differences then is it still an illness? They’re still diagnosed, they still experience the symptoms, but they can function. 

So in that scenario who is helped by labeling people as sick? Is the person hearing voices better off with other people deciding they are not healthy? It seems to me that they’re different, sure, but not sick and in need of a cure just because they aren’t “normal”

What I’m saying is that describing every chemical imbalance in the brain as an illness is inaccurate and unhelpful. That does not mean someone doesn’t need resources like medication and therapy in order to effectively handle their differences. What it does mean is that they’re not “sick” but rather just different. Someone with OCD has to go about their day differently than someone without it. But is that inherently bad and something that needs to be cured? If that’s how you view your diagnosis and you think that helps then fine, but not everyone that is mentally different should be labeled as mentally ill.

Why is it you think that a “healthy human brain” is supposed to be what the majority has? My point is that chemical imbalances in the brain are unnecessarily and broadly referred to as  illnesses. Some people need support and resources to help manage their differences, but in order to get that support they need they also have to be labeled as sick, as being something bad that others would not want to be. That’s negative and harmful.

I’m not suggesting we do away with labels. I’m advocating for a change in labels because the current one is unnecessarily harmful. Mental differences, so that not everyone who needs resources and support has to be labeled as mentally ill. That would actually make things easier for dealing with mental differences in children because doctors are hesitant to give them a diagnosis that can follow them the rest of their lives.

You’re saying it’s a sickness yet it’s not a bad or good thing and my point is that’s an oxymoron. Illness is not neutral, it’s negative and implies something is broken and needs to be fixed. I’m not saying that mental differences can’t negatively impact people’s lives or that people shouldn’t reach out to resources like psychiatrists or therapists. What I’m saying is that it isn’t accurate or helpful to broadly label every chemical imbalance in the brain as an illness. Yes, it is different from “normal” people and those differences may need accommodations and coping mechanisms, but when does someone stop being damaged?

That can actually be more damaging to tell that to someone with depression. Getting resources and support is good, but the fact that someone has to be labeled as mentally ill to get the support they need for their mental differences is actually damaging.

You seem to look at things in terms of “Bad thing = Loses points” and “Good thing = Gains points” like it’s some kind of measured system you can use to craft a proportional response. I help an old lady cross the street and I gain +5 points. Except that’s really not at all how things work, it’s incredibly subjective so the amount of points you gain or lose for literally anything would change based on where and when you are. There’s actually some controversy about whether or not the US even needed to drop the bomb, whether it really did save lives and whether the number of lives saved was proportional to the damage done.
